lessons.title: AI basics and heat detection
lessons.html:
What is artificial insemination?

Artificial insemination (AI) means placing semen collected from a selected male into the reproductive tract of a female by hand, without natural mating. It is widely used in dairy herds, increasingly in beef herds, and also in pigs, sheep and goats.

Advantages

  • Access to top bulls or boars at a fraction of the cost of buying them.
  • Faster genetic improvement in milk yield, growth, fertility or carcass traits.
  • Fewer dangerous breeding males on the farm.
  • Lower risk of spreading venereal diseases such as trichomoniasis and vibriosis.
  • Accurate breeding records and planned calving seasons.

Disadvantages

  • Needs good heat detection, handling facilities and trained staff.
  • Poor technique or poor semen handling gives low conception rates.

Heat detection is the key

Most AI failures start with missed or wrongly identified heats. The main sign in a cow is standing to be mounted. Secondary signs are mounting others, clear stringy mucus, a swollen vulva, restlessness, bellowing and ruffled tail-head hair. Use tail paint, heat-mount patches or teaser animals as aids, and observe at least twice a day for 20 to 30 minutes, early morning and late afternoon.

Timing

Many farms use the AM/PM rule for cattle: a cow first seen standing in the morning is inseminated that afternoon or evening; one first seen in the afternoon is inseminated the next morning. Timing for pigs, sheep and goats differs, and synchronisation programmes using hormones have fixed timetables. Follow the protocol from your vet or AI supplier exactly.

Record the cow's number and the time standing heat was first seen.

lessons.title: Handling semen and equipment
lessons.html:
The liquid nitrogen tank

Frozen semen is stored in straws in a tank of liquid nitrogen at about minus 196 degrees Celsius. Semen that warms even briefly and is refrozen can be damaged or killed.

  • Check the nitrogen level regularly with a measuring stick and refill before it gets low.
  • Keep the tank upright, in a cool, ventilated, locked place, off a concrete floor (on a wooden pallet), away from direct sun.
  • Never lift a canister above the frost line in the neck of the tank. Find the straw quickly and use forceps; if it takes longer than a few seconds, lower the canister back and try again.
  • Keep an up-to-date inventory of which bull is in which canister.

Safety with liquid nitrogen

  • Liquid nitrogen causes severe cold burns. Wear protective gloves and eye protection.
  • Never seal it in a closed container; it expands and can explode.
  • In a small closed room it can displace oxygen. Use it only in ventilated areas.

Thawing and loading

  1. Prepare everything first: thaw flask at the temperature stated by the semen supplier, clean paper towel, warmed AI gun, sheaths, gloves and lubricant.
  2. Remove the straw with forceps, shake off nitrogen, and place it in the thaw water for the time the supplier specifies.
  3. Dry the straw, check the bull name and code, cut the end square and load it into the warmed gun with a sheath.
  4. Protect the loaded gun from cold, sun and dirt, for example inside your clothing, and inseminate within the time the supplier recommends.

Never thaw straws in your mouth or pocket, and never refreeze a thawed straw.

lessons.title: Inseminating and keeping records
lessons.html:
Restraint and hygiene

Restrain the cow in a crush or AI stall where she is calm and secure, with a bar behind her to protect you. Never stand directly behind an unrestrained cow. Wear a long arm glove and use lubricant. Clean the vulva with a dry paper towel; never use disinfectant on the vulva or gun, as it kills semen.

Rectovaginal technique in cattle

  1. Insert the gloved, lubricated hand into the rectum and remove dung gently.
  2. Locate and hold the cervix, a firm, ridged structure about the size of a thumb or larger.
  3. Insert the gun into the vulva, angled upward first to avoid the urethral opening, then level.
  4. Guide the cervix over the gun with the hand in the rectum. Do not force the gun.
  5. When the tip has just passed through the cervix into the uterine body, deposit the semen slowly.
  6. Withdraw the gun gently and check the sheath for blood or pus, which you should report.

This skill can only be learned through hands-on training by an accredited provider under supervision; reading is not enough. AI in sheep and goats often requires vet procedures, and pig AI uses a different catheter technique.

Records

  • Female number, date and time of heat and of insemination.
  • Bull or boar name and code, and the technician.
  • Any problems observed.

Watch for return to heat about three weeks later and arrange pregnancy diagnosis by the vet. Calculate conception rate (pregnant females divided by females inseminated) to monitor results.

Equipment care

Clean and dry the gun after use, dispose of sheaths and gloves properly, and keep supplies clean and dry.

Key points

  • Accurate heat detection and correct timing drive AI success.
  • Keep semen below the frost line and never refreeze a thawed straw.
  • Liquid nitrogen causes cold burns and must be used with gloves, eye protection and ventilation.
  • Follow the supplier's thawing instructions and protect the loaded gun.
  • Deposit semen just past the cervix without force.
  • Record every insemination and follow up with pregnancy testing.
